question: A study by the University of Texas, presented on 19 October 2025 at the European Society of Medical Oncology Congress, shows that patients with advanced lung cancers or melanoma who received an mRNA vaccine against COVID-19 within 100 days of the start of their immunotherapy had their survival almost doubled compared to unvaccinated patients.

This finding comes in a context in which the EU invested heavily in the development and procurement of mRNA vaccines during the pandemic, demonstrating its capacity to coordinate when it comes to major public health challenges. 1.

Does the Commission intend to support a Europe-wide clinical trial to assess the effectiveness of mRNA vaccination against COVID-19 in combination with immunotherapy, along the lines of the exceptional coordination implemented during the pandemic?
Could the establishment of derogations or accelerated procedures under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014 on clinical trials be envisaged for such a project of public interest?

Can the European Medicines Agency facilitate an accelerated scientific assessment procedure to extend the indication of existing mRNA vaccines to their use in combination with immunotherapy, given the already established safety profile of these vaccines and the urgent oncological need?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.1.2026) The Commission is aware of the scientific study mentioned by the Honourable Member1. The Seventh Framework Programme for Research and Innovation2 and Horizon 20203 supported research on mRNA vaccines as part of a EUR 254 million research and innovation portfolio on cancer immunotherapy4.

Horizon Europe5 provides funding opportunities for research and innovation combining cancer immunotherapy and COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, e.g., under the EU Cancer Mission6, ‘Health’ Cluster 17, and Innovative Health Initiative8. The authorisation of clinical trials is a Member State competence. The Clinical Trials Regulation (CTR)9 provides maximum timelines for the authorisation procedure of clinical trials.

Member States can shorten the assessment period should they consider the need. The Commission has proposed amendments to the CTR in the context of its proposal for an EU Biotech Act10 to accelerate authorisation of clinical trials and improve patients’ access to medicines.

A company can apply for a marketing authorisation to the European Medicines Agency (EMA) with evidence to comply with the requirements of the EU legislation. This can include a justified request for accelerated assessment if the product is of significant public health interest11.
